claim: 82.6% of all Patreon campaigns ever registered between May 2013 and October 2015 never received a single pledge: 115,183 of 139,366.
stance_target: The overwhelming majority of people who attempt paid content creation earn nothing at all
scope_conditions: Complete Patreon transaction record May 2013 to October 2015; the dataset is a database dump leaked via unauthorised access in October 2015, which Patreon acknowledges but cannot vouch for; early-platform era, before Patreon's scale-up
quoted_support: Most of the registered campaigns (115,183 out of 139,366) did not receive any pledges.
region: Not reported; Patreon 2013-2015 was overwhelmingly US/Western

claim: Approximately 250 Patreon creators - the top 1% of active campaigns, and 0.18% of all registered campaigns - earned enough to constitute a living income.
stance_target: The share of creators who can live on platform earnings is a fraction of one percent
scope_conditions: Patreon 2013-2015 leaked transaction dump; 'sufficient for making a living' is the author's own judgement applied to the >USD 2,500/month tier, not a measured cost-of-living threshold; Patreon income only, excludes other creator revenue
quoted_support: Nevertheless, the top 5%, about 1200 creators, receive a substantial income and around 250 creators (the top 1%) are funded to an extent that can be considered an income sufficient for making a living.

claim: Median monthly peak earnings among Patreon campaigns that received any money at all was USD 31, while the mean was USD 197.88 - a mean six times the median.
stance_target: Typical creator earnings are trivially small and averages are dominated by the top tail
scope_conditions: 24,257 active campaigns only (excluding the 82.6% that earned nothing, which would push the true median to zero); monthly peak, not average; Patreon 2013-2015
quoted_support: A campaign’s average monthly peak pledge volume is $197.88, with the median being $31. Only 25% of the active campaigns get more than $120, 5% make more than $750 monthly and 1% more than $2500.

claim: Among Patreon campaigns that got any support at all, roughly one in five received exactly one pledge and about a third received two, so most 'successful' creators have an audience of one or two paying people.
stance_target: Crossing the threshold from zero to non-zero earnings does not indicate a viable audience
scope_conditions: 24,257 active Patreon campaigns, 2013-2015; median 5 pledges per active campaign
quoted_support: A total of 24,257 campaigns getting pledges received, on average, 39.57 (minimum 1, median 5, maximum 27,547). Around 20% of all those "active” campaigns (4930) received one pledge, around a third got two pledges.

claim: The average individual monthly pledge on Patreon was USD 11.18 with a median of USD 5, so a creator needs roughly 500 paying supporters at the median pledge to reach USD 2,500 a month.
stance_target: Quantifying the audience size required for a living income from fan funding
scope_conditions: 959,909 pledges, Patreon 2013-2015; the 500-supporter implication is arithmetic from the reported median, not stated by the author
quoted_support: The average pledge is for $11.18 (minimum 0.01, median 5, maximum 25,000) per month.

claim: Pledge-deletion patterns are highly heterogeneous across creators, with most campaigns experiencing only occasional deletions but some suffering abrupt collapses that end the campaign entirely.
stance_target: Whether creator income declines gradually or collapses
scope_conditions: Descriptive scatter-plot analysis of individual campaign trajectories; no survival curve or hazard model is fitted; the author notes the analysis cannot causally connect deletions to failure to deliver content
quoted_support: The dynamics of deletions are also quite heterogeneous ... suffered a sharp drop of its pledges at around day 130 and essentially discontinued.
numbers: day 130 collapse in the plotted example

claim: The most-cited early quantitative Patreon dataset in the academic literature derives from an unauthorised database breach rather than from platform cooperation, illustrating how far researchers must go for creator-income data.
stance_target: Creator economics research is data-starved and relies on non-standard sources
scope_conditions: Author's own disclosure footnote; Patreon acknowledges the academic use but does not warrant accuracy
quoted_support: The data has been leaked online in the course of an unauthorized access to a Patreon database in October 2015. While Patreon acknowledges our use of the data, it cannot guarantee its accuracy.
